Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
David Chen was thirty when the courthouse annex east wing collapsed inward. He had been walking the corridor toward the evidence vault, briefcase in hand, when the air suddenly thickened with the sharp, acrid scent of spilled whiskey from a nearby vendor’s cart. The sequence did not unfold in order; it arrived all at once. Shards of drywall hung in the stagnant air. A man three feet from him lay still, and David dropped to his knees, pressing his hands against a shoulder that offered no resistance. He shouted for others to come, but voices in the corridor sounded muffled, distant. By the time he dragged himself out through a collapsed stairwell, his muscles trembling with exhaustion, the concrete had settled, and the official reports would later call it a coordinated act of terrorism. To David, it was simply a space where time had fractured. In the weeks that followed, David found himself unable to reconstruct the morning. He tried to sit with his wife and explain what had happened, but the pieces would not align. He could not tell a clear story of what happened, even to himself. Instead, certain fragments would surge up, entirely vivid and unbidden. He would be standing in his kitchen, and the memory of the collapsed stairwell would feel more real than the counter in front of him, the heat of the blast pressing against his skin with a clarity that ordinary recollections never possessed. The memory felt like it was happening right now rather than something that was over. He would drop his coffee mug, heart hammering, before the present would slowly reassert itself. These intrusions quickly shaped his routine. A construction crew’s jackhammer outside his office window could freeze him mid-sentence, his body bracing against an impact that never came. He began wearing noise-canceling headphones in the courthouse, citing a migraine, when in truth he could not trust his own threshold for sudden loud noises. Alcohol became equally unbearable. When a client came to his office smelling of whiskey, David’s throat tightened, and he would abruptly excuse himself, pacing the hallway until the scent faded. Exhaustion, which had once simply meant long hours behind a deposition, now carried a different weight. After a particularly draining trial prep, he would sit on his sofa, muscles trembling with fatigue, and suddenly feel a paralyzing dread wash over him, as though his body’s surrender to tiredness mirrored the helplessness he had felt on the floor of the annex. The memory of the man in the corridor would return, and David would rehearse the moments where he should have moved faster, pulled harder, acted decisively. He had come to believe that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. Around the same time, he found himself unable to trust the people around him. He was certain that people were not what they seemed, that the casual smiles of junior associates masked hidden agendas. He began leaving work an hour early, taking back stairwells instead of elevators, scanning every lobby for structural seams. His wife noticed the distance, the way he flinched when she reached for his hand, but he could not explain the shift. What frightened him most was the realization that his own body no longer trusted the ground beneath him, making every ordinary moment feel like a countdown. Now, at thirty-three, David sits in a therapist’s office with a file folder resting on his lap. He has come because the exhaustion no longer lifts by morning, and because the courtroom has become a space he actively avoids, leaving his prosecution backlog to mount. He knows he is losing grip on the career he spent a decade building, but the alternative—continuing to navigate a world where a dropped pen or a colleague’s laughter feels like a precursor to disaster—feels impossible. What he hopes for is not to erase the past, but to find a way to carry it without his body bracing for the next blast. What he fears most is that he will spend the rest of his life waiting for permission to forgive himself.
